title: A Starbucks-Chipotle deal would be a high-stakes bet on Brian Niccol’s magic touch
excerpt: Chipotle's post-Niccol slump has made it a tempting target. But real-estate overlap may not outweigh a messy deal.
content_html:
By Joe Ciolli

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Author of the First Trade newsletter

Corporate America loves a boomerang CEO. Think Bob Iger's return to Disney, or Elliott Hill coming out of retirement for Nike.

But what Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol is apparently considering is in a category of its own.

The FT reported last week that Starbucks has explored acquiring Chipotle in what would be the restaurant industry's biggest deal ever. Here's the twist: Niccol was CEO of Chipotle before jumping to Starbucks. He could now end up buying his old company.

On Monday, Starbucks denied the reports.

"We are not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told Business Insider. "Our team is laser focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy. We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential."

Still, the idea of a Starbucks/Chipotle combo is a good excuse to look at how far both companies' stock prices have diverged since Niccol's move to Starbucks was announced in August 2024. Starbucks became a turnaround story, while Chipotle struggled to replace the man who helped make it one.

The chart below shows the dynamic in action: Chipotle has fallen an eye-watering 43% over the period, while Starbucks is up roughly 18% — though it has still lagged the S&P 500's 46% gain.

Chipotle's slump reflects more than Niccol's departure, of course. The chain has also faced softer sales, higher costs, and food-safety headaches. But the gap makes it look like a tempting turnaround target — especially to the exec who helped build it and knows it better than almost anyone.

The CEO premium comes full circle

On the surface, the combo of Starbucks and Chipotle sounds like some sort of cursed menu experiment. Pumpkin-spice burrito, anyone? But this is less a coffee-and-burrito synergy story than a CEO-conviction trade.

That makes the strongest rationale for the deal not any sort of ill-fated food concoction, but Niccol himself. He's already proven he can improve restaurant operations, refresh a brand, and drive investor excitement.

His "Back to Starbucks" effort has begun to win over the market, and buying Chipotle would allow him to apply a version of that same playbook to the company he once ran.

There's also significant overlap between the chains' real-estate footprints. About 90% of US Chipotle locations are within one mile of a Starbucks, according to research from Stephens analyst Jim Salera. That could create opportunities for shared real-estate development, better site selection, and a more powerful combined loyalty program, he added.

The deal math still looks messy

Even with those elements in mind, a possible Starbucks-Chipotle deal is still a long way from making financial sense.

The two companies have very different supply chains, customer needs, and operating models. Analysts are questioning whether what they see as modest cost savings can justify such a large price tag, especially with Starbucks in the middle of its own turnaround.

The initial reaction captured that tension. Chipotle jumped 6% Thursday on the takeover speculation, but gave back 3% Friday. Starbucks, meanwhile, fell 3% over the two days. That's not a ringing endorsement of a burrito-coffee conglomerate. It's just an intriguing possibility that investors aren't yet sold on.

Still, the rumor has already revived an intriguing market question: Is Brian Niccol's real asset Starbucks, or is it the ability to make any restaurant chain feel like a comeback story?
